title: What Is Salvation?
subtitle: Grace, repentance, faith, and righteous action in Islam and Christianity
summary: Christianity and Islam both reject the idea that human beings can save themselves without God's mercy. Christianity commonly connects salvation to Jesus's atoning death and resurrection. Islam teaches direct repentance to the one God, personal responsibility, sincere faith, righteous action, and complete dependence on divine mercy. The central question is whether forgiveness requires an inherited sacrifice or whether God can forgive those who return to Him directly.

sections.title: Salvation in Islam and Christianity
sections.body: Both faiths teach that sin is serious and that God's mercy is indispensable. Their difference concerns how mercy reaches the sinner. Christianity commonly places the cross at the center of salvation. Islam teaches that no soul bears another's guilt, that repentance is made directly to God, and that faith must produce righteous action. This gives hope without inherited guilt and accountability without despair.

sections.title: The Question Behind Salvation
sections.body: Salvation asks how a morally responsible person can be forgiven and brought near to God. A useful comparison must avoid two caricatures: Christianity is not simply permission to sin after professing faith, and Islam is not a cold system in which points purchase Paradise. Both traditions speak about grace, faith, obedience, repentance, and judgment, but they organize those ideas differently.

sections.title: Does Forgiveness Require an Atoning Death?
sections.body: The decisive disagreement is not whether God is merciful. It is whether divine justice requires Jesus to bear the penalty of others. Mainstream Christianity answers through the cross. Islam answers that God created human beings morally accountable, accepts sincere repentance, and needs no innocent victim before He can forgive. Each person bears what he or she earns, while every good outcome still depends on God's mercy.

sections.title: Christian Understandings of Grace and Works
sections.body: Christians agree that salvation begins with God's grace, but Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions describe the relation of faith, sacraments, obedience, and perseverance differently. Those differences should be represented fairly. They also show why isolated slogans such as 'faith alone' do not capture the whole New Testament, which includes both Paul's emphasis on grace and James's warning that faith without works is dead.

sections.title: The Quran: Mercy, Repentance, and Responsibility
sections.body:
The Quran joins hope and responsibility. God says:

قُلْ يَٰعِبَادِىَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا۟ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ لَا تَقْنَطُوا۟ مِن رَّحْمَةِ ٱللَّهِ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ ٱلذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًا ۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلْغَفُورُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ

'Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful' (Quran 39:53).

Forgiveness is therefore direct and open to the repentant. The Quran also states that no bearer of burdens bears another's burden (6:164) and repeatedly joins belief with righteous deeds. Deeds do not force God to grant Paradise; they reveal living faith and are judged by the One whose mercy exceeds human achievement.

sections.title: The New Testament: Grace, Faith, and Obedience
sections.body: Ephesians 2:8–9 says, 'For by grace you have been saved through faith ... not of works, that no one would boast.' James 2:17 adds, 'Faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.' Jesus likewise warns, 'Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father' (Matthew 7:21). Christians reconcile these passages in different ways, but all three prevent a shallow account in which religious words replace moral obedience.

sections.title: Two Accounts of Mercy
sections.body: Christianity commonly explains forgiveness through Christ's atoning death. Islam explains it through God's own mercy, sincere repentance, and transformed conduct. The Islamic account preserves three principles together: God forgives freely; guilt is not transferred between persons; and moral choices remain meaningful. That framework is simple, direct, and consistent with the calls to repentance delivered by God's prophets.

sections.title: What Islam Does Not Teach
sections.body: Islam does not teach salvation by deeds alone. The Prophet Muhammad said that no one enters Paradise merely because of his deeds, but by God's mercy (Sahih al-Bukhari 5673). Nor does reliance on mercy make obedience optional. Repentance includes leaving sin, regretting it, seeking forgiveness, and repairing the rights of others where possible. Hope and responsibility belong together.

sections.title: Why the Islamic Account Is Compelling
sections.body: Islam presents the God of perfect justice as also perfectly able to forgive. He does not inherit guilt into a newborn child, transfer guilt to an innocent person, or require worship of a messenger. He calls every sinner to return directly to Him. This is the prophetic pattern: worship the one God, repent, live righteously, and trust His mercy.

sections.title: The Central Takeaway
sections.body: Salvation in Islam is neither self-salvation nor despair. It is a direct relationship with God built on faith, repentance, righteous action, and mercy. The Quran's invitation is open even to those who have sinned greatly: do not despair of God's mercy, but return to Him sincerely.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Does Islam teach that a person must earn Paradise through good deeds alone, with no grace involved?
A: No. While the Quran repeatedly pairs belief with righteous deeds as the formula for reward (2:25; 103:3), it also grounds the whole system in God's mercy, promising that He "forgives all sins" for anyone who sincerely turns back to Him (39:53). Deeds matter, but so does mercy.

Q: Does mainstream Christianity teach that good works are unnecessary once a person believes?
A: No mainstream Christian tradition teaches this. Ephesians 2:8-9 teaches that salvation is a gift received by faith, not earned by works, but James 2:17 insists that real faith always produces works, and Jesus warns in Matthew 7:21 that only those who do the Father's will enter the Kingdom of Heaven.

Q: Does Islam have an equivalent to Christ's atoning death?
A: No. Islam holds that each person stands directly accountable to God for their own belief and deeds, with repentance and God's mercy sufficient for forgiveness, and no intermediary or substitutionary sacrifice required.

Q: What does Quran 2:62 mean about Jews, Christians, and Sabeans being saved?
A: Commentators differ. Some read it as referring to sincere monotheists who died before Muhammad's message reached them; others read it as a general principle about God rewarding sincere faith and righteousness. It is not read by mainstream scholarship as canceling the Quran's broader claim about the necessity of its own message.

Q: Do Paul and James contradict each other on faith and works?
A: Mainstream Christian scholarship generally reads them as complementary rather than contradictory: Paul addresses how salvation begins, by grace through faith rather than human merit, while James addresses what genuine faith necessarily produces, namely a changed life.

Q: Which view is correct?
A: The concluding section argues the Islamic case, while acknowledging that Christian scholarship offers its own coherent account of how grace, faith, and works relate.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **Major Themes of the Qur'an** — Fazlur Rahman. Examines the Quran's teaching on faith, righteous deeds, and the Hereafter in its own theological context.
- **Iustitia Dei: A History of the Christian Doctrine of Justification** — Alister E. McGrath. A standard academic history of how Christian thinkers have debated the relationship between grace, faith, and works.
- **What Saint Paul Really Said** — N.T. Wright. Places Paul's teaching on justification by faith back into its first-century Jewish context.
- **Is the Father of Jesus the God of Muhammad?** — Timothy George. An evangelical Christian scholar's respectful comparison of core Christian and Islamic doctrines, including salvation.

faq.question: Does Islam teach that a person must earn Paradise through good deeds alone, with no grace involved?
faq.answer: No. Deeds matter, but the Prophet taught that entry into Paradise is ultimately through God's mercy, not a wage forced from Him.

faq.question: Does mainstream Christianity teach that good works are unnecessary once a person believes?
faq.answer: No. Christian traditions differ about justification, but all major traditions expect genuine faith to produce obedience and moral transformation.

faq.question: Does Islam have an equivalent to Christ's atoning death?
faq.answer: No. Islam teaches direct repentance and rejects transferred guilt: each soul answers for itself, and God forgives whom He wills with justice and mercy.

faq.question: What does Quran 2:62 mean about Jews, Christians, and Sabeans being saved?
faq.answer: It affirms that God's judgment is just and that faithful obedience to genuine revelation is not ignored. The Quran also calls later communities to accept God's final messenger once his message reaches them faithfully.

faq.question: Do Paul and James contradict each other on faith and works?
faq.answer: Christians normally harmonize them by saying that salvation is by grace and that living faith necessarily bears fruit. The passages nevertheless show why faith cannot be reduced to a verbal claim.

faq.question: Which view is correct?
faq.answer: The article presents the evidence for comparison. Islam's case is that direct forgiveness, personal responsibility, and God's unrestricted mercy fit the teaching of prophetic monotheism without requiring transferred guilt.
